newsitem.title: USA: Hollywood rolls out big guns for summer movies.
newsitem.headline: Hollywood rolls out big guns for summer movies.

text.p: Splash, flash and a lot of cash. These are the features marking this summer's roster of movies and the qualities that film studios hope will produce billions of dollars in ticket sales.

Last year the film business raked in a record $2.4 billion in summer box office receipts, or 40 percent of the year's total take, by rolling out blockbuster action films such as "Independence Day," "Twister" and "Mission: Impossible."
This season, Hollywood's major studios are turning to some of the industry's biggest names to try to top that figure.

Producer-director Steven Spielberg returns with a sequel to the megahit "Jurassic Park." Arnold Schwarzenegger sheds his good guy image to play the villainous Mr. Freeze in "Batman & Robin" and Walt Disney Co. will mount a huge promotional push for its animated feature "Hercules."
But the summer of 1997 is also the most expensive season yet, making it one of the most financially perilous on record.
"The risk is substantial on some titles, but on others like 'Hercules' or 'Batman' it is less," said industry expert Harold Vogel, of New York-based financial firm Cowen & Co.
At least seven films cost near or over $100 million to make. That figure excludes promotion and advertising costs that often can double a movie's price tag.

Already, one film, director James Cameron's "Titanic", may be capsized. The film is scheduled to sail into theatres on July 2, but editing problems may delay the launch and boost its budget to around the $200 million mark.

At that price "Titanic" would join "Waterworld," Kevin Costner's 1995 flop that cost over $170 million, as one of Hollywood's most expensive movies ever. Officials at Paramount Pictures, the U.S. distributor, were not available to comment.
Despite the risks, the financial rewards can be great.
Last year, alien-busting "Independence Day" was a smash hit, grossing more than $300 million in the United States and $500 million to date worldwide.

"Jurassic Park," the all-time king of special effects and box office success, has grossed over $1 billion worldwide since the summer of 1993. The sequel, "Jurassic Park: The Lost World" hits theatres at the Memorial Day holiday and, like its predecessor, depicts modern-day dinosaurs seeking revenge on the humans who've engineered their rebirth.

June is filled with high-action, high-adventure thrillers, starting with another sequel, "Speed 2: Cruise Control", starring Sandra Bullock. With co-star Jason Patric, she must halt an out-of-control cruise ship steaming toward a Caribbean island.
Also in June, Warner Bros. launches its fourth "Batman" movie. George Clooney, star of the television's "E.R.," now plays the caped crusader, replacing Val Kilmer who was in 1995's "Batman Forever".
For moviegoers not interested in big-budget action movies, there is Julia Roberts' latest vehicle, "My Best Friend's Wedding."
In the romantic comedy, Roberts plays a woman who tries to sabotage the wedding of her best male friend, played by Dermot Mulroney, for whom she secretly pines.
It is scheduled to open in late June on the same weekend as "Face Off," an action-thriller starring Oscar winner Nicholas Cage and John Travolta.
In early July, "Men In Black" in which Will Smith and Tommy Lee Jones play government agents who track aliens on Earth, is set to open against the still unsettled "Titanic."

About a week later, Oscar winner Jodie Foster takes her first turn at an extraterrestrial story line in "Contact." July also will see the thrillers "Air Force One" starring Harrison Ford and "Conspiracy Theory" with Mel Gibson.
